questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: She has been waiting __________ the bus stop since 8 o'clock.
questions.explanation: 'At' is correct because we use 'at' with specific points or locations (bus stop, station, airport). 'In' is wrong — 'in' is used for enclosed spaces (in a room, in a city). 'On' is wrong — 'on' is used for surfaces or transport (on the bus). 'By' is wrong — 'by' indicates proximity (by the door) or an agent, not a stationary location like a bus stop.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about prepositions of time:

(i) 'At' is used with specific times (at 5 o'clock, at noon).
(ii) 'In' is used with months, years, and longer periods (in January, in 2025).
(iii) 'On' is used with days and dates (on Monday, on 15 August).
(iv) 'At' is used with months and seasons (at January, at summer).

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'at' is used with precise times (at 3 PM, at midnight). (ii) is correct — 'in' is used with months, years, seasons, centuries (in March, in 2020). (iii) is correct — 'on' is used with specific days and dates (on Friday, on 26 January). (iv) is wrong — we say 'in January' and 'in summer', not 'at January' or 'at summer'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The book is __________ the table.
questions.explanation: 'On' is correct because we use 'on' to indicate something resting on a surface. 'At' is wrong — 'at' refers to a point/location, not a surface. 'In' is wrong — 'in' indicates inside something. 'By' is wrong — 'by' means beside or near, not resting on a surface.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): We say 'interested in' and not 'interested at' or 'interested on'.
Reason (R): Certain adjectives have fixed preposition collocations in English that must be memorised.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — 'interested in' is the only correct collocation. Reason (R) is correct — English has fixed adjective + preposition combinations that don't follow general rules. (R) explains (A) because the fixed collocation nature of 'interested in' is precisely why other prepositions are unacceptable.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following prepositions with their correct usage:

Column I:
(a) between
(b) among
(c) beside
(d) besides

Column II:
(i) Next to / by the side of
(ii) In addition to / apart from
(iii) Used for two persons or things
(iv) Used for more than two persons or things

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Between' is used for two items (iii). 'Among' is used for more than two (iv). 'Beside' means next to (i). 'Besides' means in addition to (ii). The second option wrongly assigns 'more than two' to 'between'. The third option wrongly swaps 'beside' and 'besides'. The fourth option wrongly assigns 'next to' to 'between'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: He apologised __________ his rude behaviour.
questions.explanation: 'Apologise for' is the correct collocation meaning to express regret for something. 'Of' is wrong — we don't say 'apologise of'. 'About' is wrong — while 'apologise about' is occasionally heard informally, 'apologise for' is the standard correct form. 'On' is wrong — 'apologise on' is not a valid collocation.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences use prepositions correctly?

(i) She is good at mathematics.
(ii) He is afraid from dogs.
(iii) They arrived at the station on time.
(iv) I am fond of reading books.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'good at' is the correct collocation. (iii) is correct — 'arrived at' and 'on time' are both correct. (iv) is correct — 'fond of' is the correct collocation. (ii) is wrong — the correct form is 'afraid of dogs', not 'afraid from dogs'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The meeting is scheduled __________ Monday.
questions.explanation: 'On' is correct because we use 'on' with days of the week (on Monday, on Friday). 'At' is wrong — 'at' is used with specific clock times. 'In' is wrong — 'in' is used with months, years, and seasons. 'By' is wrong — 'by' indicates a deadline (by Monday means before or on Monday), not a scheduled time.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about prepositions of place:

(i) 'In' is used for enclosed areas (in the room, in the city).
(ii) 'On' is used for surfaces (on the wall, on the floor).
(iii) 'At' is used for specific points (at the door, at the corner).
(iv) 'In' is used for surfaces and 'on' is used for enclosed areas.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'in' is for enclosed or larger areas. (ii) is correct — 'on' is for surfaces. (iii) is correct — 'at' is for specific points or locations. (iv) is wrong — it reverses the usage; 'in' is for enclosed areas and 'on' is for surfaces, not the other way around.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: We have been living here __________ 2015.
questions.explanation: 'Since' is correct because it is used with a specific point in time (since 2015, since Monday). 'For' is wrong — 'for' is used with a duration of time (for five years, for two hours). 'From' is wrong — 'from' is used with 'to/till' to indicate a range (from 2015 to 2020). 'By' is wrong — 'by' indicates a deadline, not a starting point.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): We say 'depend on' and not 'depend upon' in formal English.
Reason (R): 'On' and 'upon' are interchangeable in most contexts, though 'on' is more common in everyday usage.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: (A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is not correct — both 'depend on' and 'depend upon' are acceptable in formal English; neither is wrong. Reason (R) is correct — 'on' and 'upon' are largely interchangeable, with 'on' being more common in everyday speech. Since (A) is wrong but (R) is right, the correct answer is '(A) is not correct but (R) is correct'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The cat jumped __________ the wall.
questions.explanation: 'Over' indicates movement from one side to the other of an obstacle (the cat jumped across/above the wall). 'On' is wrong — 'on' would mean the cat landed on the surface of the wall, not cleared it. 'In' is wrong — 'in' means inside the wall, which is impossible. 'At' is wrong — 'at' indicates direction toward but not the crossing movement.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following verb + preposition collocations with their meanings:

Column I:
(a) look after
(b) look for
(c) look into
(d) look forward to

Column II:
(i) To investigate
(ii) To take care of
(iii) To search for something
(iv) To anticipate with pleasure

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Look after' means to take care of (ii). 'Look for' means to search for (iii). 'Look into' means to investigate (i). 'Look forward to' means to anticipate with pleasure (iv). The second option wrongly assigns 'search' to 'look after'. The third option wrongly assigns 'investigate' to 'look for'. The fourth option wrongly assigns 'anticipate' to 'look after'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: She insisted __________ paying the bill herself.
questions.explanation: 'Insist on' is the correct verb + preposition collocation. 'For' is wrong — 'insist for' is grammatically incorrect. 'To' is wrong — 'insist to' is not standard; we say 'insist on doing' not 'insist to do'. 'At' is wrong — 'insist at' is not a valid collocation.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about prepositions of direction:

(i) 'To' indicates movement towards a destination (go to school).
(ii) 'Into' indicates movement from outside to inside (walked into the room).
(iii) 'Towards' indicates direction of movement without necessarily reaching it.
(iv) 'To' and 'towards' have exactly the same meaning with no difference.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'to' shows movement to a destination. (ii) is correct — 'into' shows entering an enclosed space. (iii) is correct — 'towards' shows direction without implying arrival. (iv) is wrong — 'to' implies reaching the destination while 'towards' only shows the direction of movement.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The boy was punished __________ his misbehaviour.
questions.explanation: 'Punished for' is the correct collocation indicating the reason for punishment. 'Of' is wrong — 'punished of' is not standard English. 'With' is wrong — 'punished with' refers to the instrument of punishment (punished with a cane), not the reason. 'By' is wrong — 'punished by' refers to the person who punishes (punished by the teacher), not the reason.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: He is not capable __________ handling this responsibility.
questions.explanation: 'Capable of' is the fixed adjective + preposition collocation. 'For' is wrong — we don't say 'capable for'. 'To' is wrong — while 'able to' is correct, 'capable to' is non-standard; the correct form is 'capable of + gerund'. 'In' is wrong — 'capable in' is not a valid collocation.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The children are playing __________ the park.
questions.explanation: 'In' is correct because a park is an enclosed/defined area, and 'in' is used for larger areas. 'On' is wrong — 'on' is used for surfaces, not areas. 'At' is wrong — 'at' is used for specific points; for a park (a larger space) 'in' is preferred. 'Into' is wrong — 'into' implies movement from outside to inside, but they are already playing there.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following adjective + preposition collocations are correct?

(i) proud of
(ii) angry with (a person)
(iii) satisfied from
(iv) different from

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'proud of' is the standard collocation. (ii) is correct — 'angry with a person' is correct. (iv) is correct — 'different from' is the accepted standard form. (iii) is wrong — the correct form is 'satisfied with', not 'satisfied from'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The train arrived __________ the platform on time.
questions.explanation: 'Arrived at' is correct because 'arrive' uses 'at' for specific locations/points (arrived at the station, at the platform). 'On' is wrong — we don't say 'arrived on the platform' for reaching a place. 'In' is wrong — 'arrive in' is used for cities/countries (arrived in Delhi). 'To' is wrong — we say 'arrived at' not 'arrived to' in standard English.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): We say 'at night' but 'in the morning'.
Reason (R): English uses 'at' for night because night is considered a point in time, while morning/afternoon/evening are treated as periods.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — 'at night' and 'in the morning' are the standard forms. Reason (R) is correct — the traditional explanation is that 'night' is treated as a point while other parts of day are treated as periods. (R) explains (A) because this point-vs-period distinction is why different prepositions are used.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: She congratulated him __________ his success.
questions.explanation: 'Congratulate on' is the correct verb + preposition collocation. 'For' is wrong — while 'for' can sometimes appear informally, 'congratulate on' is the standard form. 'At' is wrong — 'congratulate at' is not valid. 'About' is wrong — 'congratulate about' is not a standard collocation.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about 'since' and 'for':

(i) 'Since' is used with a specific point in time (since Monday, since 2010).
(ii) 'For' is used with a duration or period of time (for two hours, for five years).
(iii) 'Since' and 'for' are interchangeable in all contexts.
(iv) Both 'since' and 'for' are commonly used with present perfect tense.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'since' marks a starting point. (ii) is correct — 'for' indicates duration. (iv) is correct — both are commonly used with present perfect (has lived here since/for). (iii) is wrong — they are NOT interchangeable; 'since 2010' is correct but 'for 2010' is wrong, and 'for five years' is correct but 'since five years' is wrong.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The thief was charged __________ robbery.
questions.explanation: 'Charged with' is the correct legal collocation (charged with a crime). 'For' is wrong — we say 'charged with', not 'charged for' a crime. 'Of' is wrong — we say 'accused of' but 'charged with'. 'On' is wrong — 'charged on' is not a valid collocation in this context.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following sentences with the correct prepositions to fill in the blanks:

Column I:
(a) He is known __________ his honesty.
(b) She is married __________ a doctor.
(c) They agreed __________ the proposal.
(d) He suffers __________ asthma.

Column II:
(i) to
(ii) from
(iii) for
(iv) to

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Known for' his honesty (iii). 'Married to' a doctor (i). 'Agreed to' the proposal (iv). 'Suffers from' asthma (ii). The second option wrongly assigns 'to' for 'known'. The third option wrongly assigns 'from' for 'married'. The fourth option wrongly assigns 'to' for 'suffers'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The bus left __________ time.
questions.explanation: 'On time' is the correct fixed expression meaning punctually/as scheduled. 'In time' is wrong in this context — 'in time' means with time to spare (arrived in time for the show), which has a different meaning. 'At time' is wrong — this is not a valid expression. 'By time' is wrong — this is not a standard English expression.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about prepositions with transport:

(i) We say 'by bus/train/car' (without article) for mode of transport.
(ii) We say 'on the bus' when inside a bus.
(iii) We say 'in the car' when inside a car.
(iv) We say 'on the car' when inside a car.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'by + mode of transport (no article)' indicates how one travels. (ii) is correct — we say 'on the bus/train/plane' (larger vehicles you can stand in). (iii) is correct — we say 'in the car/taxi' (smaller vehicles you sit in). (iv) is wrong — 'on the car' means on the roof/surface of the car, not inside it.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: He has been absent __________ school for three days.
questions.explanation: 'Absent from' is the correct adjective + preposition collocation. 'At' is wrong — while we say 'present at', we say 'absent from', not 'absent at'. 'In' is wrong — 'absent in' is not a valid collocation. 'Of' is wrong — 'absent of' is not standard English.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences are grammatically correct in their use of prepositions?

(i) The teacher distributed books among the five students.
(ii) He divided the cake between his three friends.
(iii) She sat beside me during the ceremony.
(iv) Besides being clever, she is also hardworking.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'among' is correctly used for more than two (five students). (iii) is correct — 'beside' (next to) is used correctly. (iv) is correct — 'besides' (in addition to) is used correctly. (ii) is wrong — 'between' is traditionally used for two items; for three friends, 'among' is more appropriate.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: I shall complete this work __________ Friday.
questions.explanation: 'By Friday' is correct because 'by' indicates a deadline — the work will be done on or before Friday. 'On' is wrong — 'on Friday' means specifically on that day, not as a deadline for completion. 'Till/until' is wrong — 'until Friday' would mean the action continues up to Friday, not that it will be completed before Friday.
